newsitem.title: JORDAN: Jordan to send economic delegation to Iraq.
newsitem.headline: Jordan to send economic delegation to Iraq.

text.p: Jordan will send a senior economic team to Iraq soon to boost trade links with Baghdad after its $2 billion U.N. oil-for-food deal, Minister of Information Marwan Muasher said on Monday.

"In a short period a Jordanian delegation headed by the ministers of energy and finance will travel to Baghdad to be followed by a meeting of the joint Jordanian-Iraqi economic committee," Muasher told reporters.

The Jordanian delegation, led by Finance and Customs Minister Marwan Awad and Energy and Mineral Resources Minister Hashem Dabbas, will be the most senior official mission to Iraq since King Hussein last year turned against President Saddam Hussein after years of close ties.

Officials say the visit is prompted by concern about losing out to other regional neighbours in stepped up competition by Turkey, Gulf states and international businessmen to gain a share of the lucrative oil-for-food deal.
The deal, signed on May 20 with the United Nations, allows Iraq to sell $2 billion worth of oil in a renewable six month period to raise money to buy food and medicine for Iraqis.

The last Jordanian ministerial delegation was headed by former energy minister Samih Darwazah, who went to Baghdad in September 1995 to renew an annual oil supply deal under which Jordan meets most of its energy needs.
Jordan imports 75,000 barrels per day of crude oil and byproducts from Iraq at reduced rates.
No Jordanian official has been sent to Iraq since that visit, which came one month after senior Iraqis defected and were sheltered by King Hussein.
King Hussein has recently backed down from open calls for a change in regime in Iraq and senior officials have sent more conciliatory gestures towards Baghdad.
Many ordinary Jordanians still have strong ties with their neighbour and continue to trade with Iraq under an annual protocol covering humanitarian goods exempted from the sanctions.

Jordan, a traditional trading partner of Iraq and a transit route for many of its imports, has suffered from the six-year-old U.N. embargo on its neighbour imposed after Iraq's 1990 invasion of Kuwait. Jordanian industry lost a major export market and business at Aqaba port plummeted.
Many businessmen are pinning hopes on revived trade with Iraq to help activate a stagnant industrial sector that grew primarily to cater for the needs of the Iraqi market.

Prime Minister Abdul-Karim al-Kabariti met Iraqi Trade Minister Mohammed Mehdi Saleh who was passing through Amman on Saturday, Muasher said, adding that he would meet him again on Wednesday on his way back to Baghdad.
"The Prime Minister discussed during the meeting the mechanism of the implementation of U.N. resolution 986 generally and foodstuffs and drugs allowed in return for oil sales," Muasher said.
